endorsements.quote: By involving end users in usability testing and other design activities—particularly those with varying language preferences, cultural norms, and digital and health literacy—developers can ensure GenAI-supported tools are tailored to account for the unique preferences, contexts, communication styles, and needs of individual patients [ 68 69 ].
To capitalize on GenAI’s ability to support the PC CDS use cases illustrated in this manuscript, engaging patients and caregivers during the design and development process is essential [ 67 ].
To ensure the quality and safety of GenAI-supported PC CDS, developers must rigorously evaluate and independently test processes before deployment [ 74 ].

GenAI algorithms and the data they operate on evolve, necessitating reassessment by the organization implementing GenAI-supported PC CDS to identify and address algorithmic drift, where shifts in data patterns lead to degraded performance or unintended outputs [ 74 ].
Monitoring must therefore address behaviors such as hallucinations [ 79 ], reasoning quality [ 80 ], sycophantic behavior [ 81 ], and input robustness or feature drift [ 82 ].

For GenAI-supported PC CDS, outcomes and fairness can be assessed using similar principles, that is, evaluating whether recommendations lead to desired clinical and safety outcomes overall and across patient subgroups.

Organizations should establish clear triggers for reassessment—such as major guideline updates, new evidence affecting care recommendations, demographic changes in the patient population, the passage of time, or early signals of performance deterioration—and establish a reassessment frequency based on the clinical risk and operational impact of the GenAI-supported application [ 84 85 ].
Patients need clear explanations of when and how GenAI is used in PC CDS tools that influence their care, along with the technology’s limitations [ 86 ].
Patients should have the right to opt out of the use of GenAI in their care and have full knowledge of who will access their data and how it will be used if they choose to participate.

Risk-based guardrails should define when GenAI can operate autonomously in supporting patients’ knowledge and data capture (eg, by translating clinician-authored recommendations into plain language, generating visit summaries, or helping patients record symptoms and goals for minor issues) and where clinician review and sign-off are required before outputs are used to guide care (eg, for patients with multimorbidities who may face conflicting guidelines) [ 74 ].

Critical health AI literacy, the ability to critically evaluate GenAI outputs, recognizing how health systems and structural factors may shape them, and using this awareness to make informed decisions, is an emerging concept that can complement organizational safeguards by helping patients engage more safely and effectively with GenAI PC CDS [ 76 ].

unlisted_practices: Develop patient-centered transparency and consent guidelines, including consideration of dynamic consent models for adaptive GenAI systems.
Adapt models such as the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments for AI to require local oversight of GenAI tools.
Design monitoring approaches and metrics that are feasible and usable by clinical and organizational leaders, not just data scientists.
Use human-in-the-loop clinician support to help patients with low digital health literacy interpret patient-facing GenAI outputs.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint paper presenting research and practice considerations and recommendations for integrating GenAI into patient-centered clinical decision support.
